title: The Iran War Has Slipped Into a Dangerous Limbo
text:
P resident Trump appears content, for now, to leave the Iran war in an indefinite holding pattern. By avoiding both military strikes and peace talks, he hopes to allow time for the naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz and extensive U.S. sanctions to squeeze the regime into submission. Trump believes he can afford to wait because Washington holds all the leverage. “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” Trump recently wrote on social media. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

 Tehran has a mirror-image view. The regime believes that it holds the leverage, especially after dissatisfaction with the war and sky-high gas prices led to a rout of Republicans in the midterm elections. Iran, like the Trump administration, believes that its position will grow stronger over time. Its leaders are prepared to maintain the status quo, driving up the costs of the war for the United States and its allies by launching periodic drone attacks and cyberattacks. Last week, the head of the Supreme National Security Council said Iran would not allow the removal of “even a single particle of enriched nuclear material,” a position hardly designed to coax the Trump administration into negotiations. (One of the few things the president has been consistent about in the war is his determination to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.)

 The upshot of both parties playing the waiting game is that the conflict appears to have stabilized. But that’s misleading. The greatest danger now is a dramatic escalation through a miscalculation, an accident, or a rash attempt by either side to capitalize on what it considers its advantage. Beneath the apparent calm, the standoff remains deeply unstable. Trump’s Iran-war plans are in limbo because limbo is better than the other options. But that limbo can’t last forever.

 I n the weeks before the midterms, Trump privately told people that he favored another round of military strikes so severe that Iran would have no choice but to reopen negotiations. But this time, they would be on Washington’s terms, finally granting Trump the victory he has long claimed to have already won. Trump appears to have cooled on the idea in recent days. “There just aren’t many good options right now,” one outside adviser told us. And the midterms “made it worse.”

 There is also a resigned sense in the West Wing that Trump’s leverage over Iran has diminished, however much he tries to pretend otherwise. Tehran can follow the news. The Democrats’ sweep was a sharp rebuke to the president. Some in the White House fear that hard-liners in Iran will interpret the result just as many pundits in the U.S. did: as evidence that the American public has little appetite for a prolonged conflict and that Trump will eventually be forced to cut his losses.

 The Republican Thomas Massie’s unsuccessful bid to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which was driven in part by Hegseth’s handling of the Iran war, reinforced the political risks that Trump could face were he to resume a full-scale conflict. Hence the focus on squeezing Tehran economically as the least unpalatable option. “Eventually you have to eat,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters last week. “Eventually the economic realities penetrate the skull of even the most radical lunatic.”

 [ Read: Democrats are ready to run Hegseth ‘out of town’ ] 

 But how much longer can the administration afford to wait? The massive military deployment is costly, strains personnel and equipment, and ties up assets that could be deployed elsewhere. About 17 U.S. Navy warships are in the Middle East, including three aircraft-carrier groups, the third having recently arrived from Asia. (Whether the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived to relieve one of the other two or to complement them is unclear.) The naval blockade has operated, off and on, since April. But shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains far below normal levels. The U.S. recently launched a separate operation, dubbed Task Force Iron Gate, to disrupt the trading of weapons, dual-use technologies, and other sanctioned materials through overland routes. But interdiction is extremely difficult.

 Trump also runs the risk of the limbo becoming, in the eyes of many inside and outside his own party, the sort of “ forever war ” that he promised never to start. He has noted that the Iran war is currently nowhere near as long as the conflicts in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Vietnam were. But his early predictions of a conflict lasting a few weeks already look naive as the war approaches its tenth month. Although the economic campaign is working in many ways, Iran’s regime has shown little regard for the well-being of its people and a surprising ability to absorb U.S. pressure. Indeed, Tehran could view ongoing conflict as a helpful tool to keep its citizens’ attention focused on outside threats, rather than the regime’s own economic and political weaknesses.

 Iran’s neighbors, meanwhile, have been discouraging Washington from resuming attacks because they fear becoming targets of Iranian retaliation. Trump, for now, seems to be heeding the message without signaling to Tehran that he is backing down. “At this point, taking military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing—but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” Trump told reporters during a White House briefing last week.

 Even if Trump changes his mind—as he has repeatedly—and resumes the full-bore conflict, renewed hostilities would not necessarily achieve a decisive blow. And at least one of the options Trump gave during a July press conference—striking water-treatment plants as part of a broadside on Iranian infrastructure—could amount to a war crime under international law. Democrats, with their new, large majorities in both chambers on Capitol Hill, could add any targeting of water-treatment plants to the list of Iran-war issues they want to investigate come January.

 I n December 2011 , Eric Schmidt, then a top executive at Google, issued an ominous warning about Iran’s cyber capabilities. Iran had just captured an American drone and was suspected of a cyberattack in Europe. “The Iranians are unusually talented in cyberwar for some reason we don’t fully understand,” Schmidt said in an interview on CNN. More than a decade later, Iran has repeatedly demonstrated its cyber capabilities through attacks. France last week accused the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ affiliated cyber unit of infiltrating refrigeration systems at roughly 700 French commercial sites in October, manipulating the controls in order to spoil food, trigger fires, and disrupt commerce. In July, Iranian-linked hackers were suspected of targeting more than 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, disrupting the regulation of pumps and treatment operations.

 [ Read: Why is everyone connecting fridges to the internet? ] 

 Those might just be a foretaste of what Tehran would unleash were the U.S. to restart military operations. Iran also retains the ability to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz with mines and drones, to threaten U.S. forces and regional allies, and to disrupt U.S. operations worldwide. Last month, a dozen B-1 bombers were relocated from a U.K. base used by the U.S. in England after threats from a group linked to Iran.

 As the U.S. and Iran posture, pressure, and harass each other, oil prices remain elevated; Brent crude is just under $100 a barrel. “It will be very hard to get back to $70 a barrel, where it was at the start of the war,” Danny Citrinowicz, a former Israeli intelligence officer who specializes in Iran, told us.

 For now, all parties seem tolerant of that awkward status quo, given the unappealing alternatives. But because of the U.S. blockade’s mounting costs, “this scenario is too unstable, too dangerous, and too costly to go in perpetuity,” Trita Parsi, a co-founder of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a think tank, told us. Something has to give.

 One possible outcome, Parsi said, is a “Swiss cheese” scenario: The United States gradually and secretly relaxes its enforcement of the blockade and sanctions, while formally keeping both in place. That could free up ships for deployment elsewhere and gradually allow more tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, increasing global energy supplies. Meanwhile, Gulf nations could begin negotiating their own arrangements with Tehran to protect against retaliatory attacks. Iran might find enough to like in this arrangement that it waits, in effect, for the holes to overwhelm the cheese. What emerges, Parsi said, could be “a new equilibrium” in which the United States can claim to be maintaining sanctions or enforcing a blockade, but does so weakly enough that “Iranians don’t have an incentive to escalate.”

 Such an arrangement might buy Trump time and prevent an immediate return to hostilities. But it would also leave him in purgatory. Trump could not credibly claim to have defeated Iran or meaningfully weakened its capabilities. Nor would he have to admit defeat by accepting Iran’s terms at the negotiating table.

 [ Read: How Trump left America vulnerable to cyberattacks ] 

 The gap between the two sides’ demands remains enormous. Washington wants an agreement that effectively dismantles Iran’s nuclear program and restores the Strait of Hormuz to a free and open waterway. Tehran wants an agreement that recognizes its effective control of the strait, lifts the sanctions, and guarantees that the United States will not attack again.

 For now, Iran and the Trump administration have found ways to avoid making difficult decisions that might lead to a clear outcome. Instead, both are betting that time is on their side. But that may be the most dangerous assumption of all.
